## The Swedish academic system 
Before diving into Open Science, it helps to understand **how research in Sweden actually works**. Laws, funding models, and institutional responsibilities shape what you as a researcher can and cannot do, often in ways that are not immediately visible in your everyday work. Knowing the basics of the Swedish research system makes it easier to understand your **rights and responsibilities** as a researcher, and provides **important context** for later discussions about sharing data, publications, and other Open Science practices.

### Who sets the rules?
At the national level, the [Government and the Riksdag (the Swedish parliament)](https://www.regeringen.se/other-languages/english---how-sweden-is-governed/) are responsible for higher education. They:

::: {.callout}
***Set the legal framework for universities and university colleges***,  mainly through two laws:   

- [The Higher Education Act](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/hogskolelag-19921434_sfs-1992-1434/), which sets out the mission of higher education, academic freedom, and institutional responsibilities 
- [The Higher Education Ordinance](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/hogskoleforordning-1993100_sfs-1993-100/), which provides more detailed rules on degrees, admissions, employment, and study programmes. 
 
The Government also sets the strategic direction for Swedish research through a national research policy bill, published every four years. [The current bill (2025–2028)](https://www.regeringen.se/rattsliga-dokument/proposition/2024/12/prop.-20242560) outlines priorities such as research excellence, internationalisation, and innovation, and shapes how public research funding is distributed.
:::

::: {.callout}
***Allocate public funding to universities, with education and research funded separately.***  
Research & PhD education funding comes from:

- Recurrent government funding (base grants to universities)
- External competitive funding, awarded by public agencies and other private research funders and organisations.  
   Almost half of all external funding comes from the Swedish government through research councils, in particular:
   - the Swedish Research Council (Vetenskapsrådet)
   - the Swedish Research Council for Health, Working Life and Welfare (Forte)
   - the Swedish Research Council for Sustainable Development (Formas)
   - Sweden’s Innovation Agency (Vinnova)
   - the Swedish Energy Agency (Energimyndigheten)
:::


::: {.callout}
***Supervise higher education and research providers to ensure compliance with national legislation***

Several (independent) government agencies under the Ministry of Education and Research are responsible for supervising universities and research activities in Sweden:

- The Swedish Higher Education Authority (Universitetskanslersämbetet, UKÄ)supervises higher education institutions to ensure they comply with applicable legislation, including the Higher Education Act, the Higher Education Ordinance, the Administrative Procedures Act, and their own internal regulations.  
- The Swedish Council for Higher Education (Universitets- och högskolerådet, UHR) works with admissions, recognition of qualifications, international mobility, and information about higher education, rather than supervision of research quality.

- **The Swedish Ethical Review Authority (Etikprövningsmyndigheten)**  
  Evaluates research involving humans, biological material, or sensitive personal data. Researchers must submit study plans for ethical review and approval before such research can begin.
:::


>🎓 **PhD takeaway:**
Your PhD is shaped by national laws, not just local practice. Funding structures influence how research is organised and public-sector rules apply to most universities.


### What is the role of universities?

Universities and university colleges have a broad mission that includes:

- Education based on research or artistic practice
- Research and development work
- Interaction with society, so that research and knowledge benefit the wider community

In addition, Swedish higher education institutions have to guarantee researchers academic freedom. This means that researchers and teachers should be free to choose research questions, methods, and how results are communicated, within the legal framework.

Although Sweden’s higher education system is nationally regulated, universities are given a lot of freedom in how research and education are carried out.  The Government sets overarching goals,
but institutions decide independently how to meet them. For early-career researchers, this means that day-to-day research life is shaped largely by your university and your role within it. Universities independently decide:

- How they are organised
- Which courses and programmes to offer
- The content and design of education
- How many students to admit
- What research to prioritise

There is thus no nationally fixed curriculum and no central planning of how much research or education should be done in specific fields. For PhD students, this also means that conditions can vary between universities.
though three academic positions – professor,
senior lecturer, and associate senior lecturer – are regulated by law.
Under the Higher Education Act, researchers are free to choose research problems, develop
methods, and publish results. The Act also emphasises academic credibility and good re
search practice, along with the responsibility of higher education institutions to safeguard
and promote academic freedom.

Part 2: Key Research Institutions and Funding Bodies
Estimated time: 15–20 minutes

Swedish National Data Service (SND)	Data repository for research data; supports data management	Researchers deposit and access data


Universities	Implement policies, supervise researchers, manage grants	Day-to-day administration of academic work
Reflection: Consider which of these institutions you interact with the most and why.
Part 3: Roles and Responsibilities
Estimated time: 10–15 minutes
Understanding who is responsible for what is key:
Researchers:
Uphold academic freedom and research integrity
Comply with legal obligations and funder requirements
Manage and report data and publications responsibly
Universities:
Support researchers with policy guidance and infrastructure
Supervise PhD students and staff
Ensure compliance with national laws and funder requirements
Funders:
Define grant conditions and priorities
Monitor compliance and reporting
Provide guidance on best practices
Tip: These roles are interlinked. A failure in one often impacts the others.
Part 4: Legal Principles Affecting Academic Work
Estimated time: 15–20 minutes
1. Lärarundantaget (Teacher’s Exemption)
Swedish law allows teachers to freely use and publish materials they create for teaching.
Implications: Teaching materials may be exempt from certain sharing obligations, but this does not override ethical or legal requirements for research data.
2. Allmän handling (Public Document)
Many documents held by public authorities (including universities) are considered public.
Principle of Public Access: Anyone may request access to official documents.
Implications: Research records, communications, and reports may be accessible unless legally restricted (e.g., privacy, sensitive data).
Tip: Researchers must balance transparency with confidentiality obligations.
Part 5: Key Policy and Guidance Documents
Estimated time: 10–15 minutes
Some of the most important national documents include:
The Higher Education Act (Högskolelagen) – governs universities, academic freedom, and responsibilities.
Swedish Research Council guidelines – includes research ethics, open access recommendations, and data management.
Freedom of the Press Act / Principle of Public Access – foundation for public access to documents.
National guidelines for research integrity – defines good scientific practice.
Exercise: Skim the Swedish Research Council website and identify one guideline relevant to your research area: https://www.vr.se
Part 6: Assignments / Knowledge Checks
Estimated time: 30–40 minutes
